To improve their performance and extend mission time, elastic and soft elements have been applied to quadrupedal robots in recent works. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Quadrupedal robots promise to address real-world challenges because of their potential advantages in mobility and versatility. To improve their performance and extend mission time, elastic and soft elements have been applied to quadrupedal robots in recent works. Stable locomotion can be achieved by off-the-shelf solvers, but achieving highly dynamic motion is still an open challenge because the dynamics are under-actuated, hybrid and nonlinear.

With trajectory optimization (TO) and model predictive control (MPC), quadrupedal robots have achieved acrobatic motions, including jumping and back-flip. But these approaches are computationally intensive and they require accurate models. To guarantee a solution when solving the TO problems, the problem formulations often need to be simplified, and this results in a conservative solution.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to model-based controllers for dynamic motions. Normal gaits like trotting can be learned from scratch easily, but learning acrobatic motions needs an extra setup, like tedious reward shaping and careful curriculum design, because the dynamics are highly nonlinear and the reward is sparse. To address this, current RL frameworks assume that prior knowledge on how to solve the task is available, as a reference motion/trajectory, a pre-existing controller or both. This reliance on expert knowledge limits how applicable these methods are, because the knowledge may not be readily available, and it can bias the learning towards sub-optimal policies.

Apart from generating motions for rigid robots, many works have argued that introducing elasticity can give better performance, but it brings extra control challenges. So far, very limited work has been done on generating highly dynamic quadrupedal motions that exploit parallel elasticity. Some RL-based works use passive elasticity for quadrupedal locomotion, but they do not report acrobatic motions like the ones in this work. The only exception is SpaceBok, but it is specifically designed to work in a low-gravity environment.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a two-stage strategy that learns highly dynamic motions from scratch by combining RL with an evolution strategy (ES), as shown in Fig. 1. First, an evolution stage directly learns joint commands that meet the task demands, without needing an expert demonstration defined in advance. In this stage we use the augmented random search (ARS) algorithm to learn a linear policy. Then we transfer the learned policy to a more expressive neural network with deep reinforcement learning (DRL). We use proximal policy optimization (PPO) to refine the policy, which is warm-started by mimicking the motions learned in the first stage. A similar two-stage method with ES and DRL has been proposed in earlier work for quadrupedal locomotion. But there the ES, specifically the natural evolution strategies algorithm, was used to search the parameters of a center pattern generator that generates reference trajectories for the second-stage RL, and no dynamic motions like ours were reported.

We validate the approach with rich simulations of learning versatile acrobatic motions, including jumping, pronking and back-flip, see Fig. 2. We also apply the approach to both a rigid and an articulated soft quadruped. We show that the proposed architecture makes it possible to exploit parallel elasticity to achieve highly dynamic motions. For example, in the jumping task, the articulated soft quadrupedal robot could jump 15.4% higher in the in-place jumping task, and 23.1% further in forward jumping.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Quadrupedal robots [1,2,3] promise to address real-world challenges thanks to their potential advantages in mobility and versatility. To improve performance and extend mission time [4], elastic and soft elements [5] have been applied to quadrupedal robots in recent works, such as [6,7,8,9]. Although stable locomotion can be achieved by off-the-shelf solvers, accomplishing highly dynamic motion is still an open challenge due to the under-actuated, hybrid, nonlinear dynamics.

Acrobatic motions have been achieved with quadrupedal robots by means of trajectory optimization (TO) and model predictive control (MPC), including jumping [10,11,12] and back-flip [13,14]. However, these approaches are computationally intensive and require accurate models. To guarantee a solution when solving the TO problems, simplifications in the problem formulations are often needed, resulting in conservative solutions.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to model-based controllers for achieving dynamic motions. Although normal gaits like trotting can easily be learned from scratch, learning acrobatic motions requires extra setup, such as tedious reward shaping [15,16,17] and careful curriculum design [18,19,20,21], due to the highly nonlinear dynamics and reward sparsity. To address this problem, current RL frameworks assume that prior knowledge on how to solve the task is available in the form of a reference motion/trajectory [22,23,24,25,26], a pre-existing controller [27,28] or both [29,30]. This reliance on expert knowledge limits the applicability of these methods, as such knowledge may not be readily available and may bias the learning towards sub-optimal policies.

Apart from motion generation for rigid robots, many works have argued that introducing elasticity can yield better performance [31], which, however, brings extra control challenges. Up to now, very limited work has been done on generating highly dynamic quadrupedal motions that exploit parallel elasticity. RL-based works such as [7] and [9] employ passive elasticity for quadrupedal locomotion but do not report acrobatic motions such as those in this work. The only exception is SpaceBok [8], which is, however, specifically designed for a low-gravity environment.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a two-stage strategy for learning highly dynamic motions from scratch by combining RL with an evolution strategy (ES), as illustrated in Fig. 1. First, an evolution stage is used to directly learn joint commands that meet the task demands, without requiring an expert demonstration defined in advance. In this stage, we use the augmented random search (ARS) [32] algorithm to learn a linear policy. Then, we transfer the learned policy to a more expressive neural network via deep reinforcement learning (DRL) [33]. We use proximal policy optimization (PPO) [34] to refine the policy, which is warm-started by mimicking the motions learned in the first stage. Note that a similar two-stage method combining ES and DRL has been proposed in [35] for quadrupedal locomotion. However, there the ES, specifically the natural evolution strategies algorithm [36], was used to search the parameters of a center pattern generator that produces reference trajectories for the second-stage RL, and no dynamic motions like ours were reported.

We validate the approach through rich simulations of learning versatile acrobatic motions, including jumping, pronking and back-flip, see Fig. 2. Furthermore, we apply the approach to both a rigid and an articulated soft quadruped. We demonstrate that the proposed architecture enables exploiting parallel elasticity to achieve highly dynamic motions. Taking the jumping task as an example, the articulated soft quadrupedal robot could jump 15.4% higher in in-place jumping, and 23.1% further in forward jumping.
